# AlgoBridge documentation

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/concepts/api-budget/ -->
# API budget

Every call AlgoBridge makes to Salesforce counts against your org's API request limit. That is true of any integration you run yourself, and it shapes the whole design. This page explains the limit, how AlgoBridge keeps within it, and how to estimate what your instance will use.

## Why every call counts

Salesforce limits how many API requests an org can make in a rolling 24 hours. An Enterprise Edition org gets 100,000 requests plus 1,000 per user licence. REST, SOAP, Bulk API and Bulk API 2.0 requests all count. Your other integrations share the same allowance.

Some hosted sync services have calls that do not count toward your API request limits. That exemption is not open to software you run yourself. AlgoBridge pays for every call, the same as any other integration in your org, and in return you get no per-row charge and a sync that runs on your own infrastructure.

So AlgoBridge treats call efficiency as a requirement, not a tuning option:

- **Never one call per record.** Reads come in pages of 2,000 records, or as Bulk API jobs. Writes go 200 records per SOAP call, or as Bulk API jobs for large runs.
- **Cheap when nothing changes.** A probe asks whether an object has changed before anything is read. See [Salesforce to PostgreSQL](salesforce-to-postgres.md#detecting-changes-probes).
- **The cheaper transport wins.** Loads and sends compare the call cost of each transport and pick the lower one.
- **A governor watches the total.** It slows and then pauses AlgoBridge before your org runs out.

## Watching usage at no cost

Salesforce reports the org's current usage on every REST response, in the `Sforce-Limit-Info` header, and in the limit information returned with SOAP responses. AlgoBridge reads it from responses it was getting anyway, so tracking usage costs nothing. It also counts its own calls by the hour, so the connection screen can show the org's total use and AlgoBridge's share of it.

## The governor

The governor compares the org's usage with two thresholds you set as instance settings.

| Org usage | State | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| below the soft threshold | **normal** | Nothing changes. |
| at or above **soft** (`sf_api_soft_percent`, default 70%) | **slowed** | Every mapping's poll interval is multiplied by 4, capped at one hour. The outbound maximum wait is multiplied by 4. The daily sweep is deferred. An API budget alert opens. |
| at or above **hard** (`sf_api_hard_percent`, default 90%) | **paused** | Probes, fetches, writes to Salesforce and new Bulk jobs all wait. The alert escalates. |
| back below soft minus 5 points | **normal** | Scheduling resumes and the alert closes. |

A few rules make the governor safe to rely on:

- **Capture never pauses.** Changes in PostgreSQL keep queuing in the change log while writes are paused, so a pause costs latency, never data.
- **The 5-point margin stops flapping.** Without it, an org sitting right on the threshold would open and close the alert on every pass.
- **Recovery is automatic.** A paused instance moves back to slowed as soon as usage drops below the hard threshold. While paused, AlgoBridge refreshes its usage reading every 10 minutes, so it notices the drop.
- **It fails open.** Before AlgoBridge has a usage reading, it runs normally rather than blocking.
- **Loads check headroom first.** An initial load or Reload weighs its estimated cost against the remaining headroom before it starts.

!!! tip "Choosing thresholds"
    The thresholds are a share of the whole org's allowance, not of AlgoBridge's own use. If other integrations already use most of your limit, lower the soft threshold so AlgoBridge backs off before they are affected.

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/api-budget-governor.html?embed=1" title="Budget governor states" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the governor states full size](../assets/diagrams/api-budget-governor.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

## Adaptive intervals

Each mapping polls on its own interval, between a minimum (default 5 minutes, allowed 2 to 60) and a maximum (default 30 minutes). After 3 empty probes in a row the interval doubles. A change resets it to the minimum. A busy object stays near the minimum; a quiet one settles at the maximum and costs few calls. The console shows each mapping's current interval and why it last changed.

## What change detection costs

The cost of finding changes depends on the change source. These figures are for 50 mapped objects.

| Change source | Calls per poll | Calls/day at a 2-minute interval | Calls/day at 5 minutes | Range across intervals |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One query per object (not used; for comparison) | 50 | 36,000 | — | — |
| Composite probe (default) | 10 (5 objects per call) | 7,200 | about 2,900 | about 480 to 7,200 |
| Apex probe | 1 (up to 90 objects) | 720 | about 290 | about 48 to 720 |
| Change notifier | 0 per change | — | — | about 25 a day: an hourly fallback poll plus 1 daily check |

On top of detection, each change source pays for:

- **Fetches.** About 1 call per 2,000 changed records, and at least 1 call for each object a probe finds changed.
- **The daily check** that your change source still works: 1 call a day.
- **The daily sweep.** One Bulk query per mapping, about 5 calls per mapping per day.

The [Change notifier](change-notifier.md) page breaks down its costs in full.

## Estimating your calls per day

Add up five parts:

| Part | How to estimate it |
|---|---|
| Detection | (objects ÷ objects per call, rounded up) × polls per day. Polls per day = 86,400 ÷ the interval in seconds. |
| Fetch | For each poll that finds changes: changed objects × (changed records ÷ 2,000, rounded up). |
| Sweep | 5 × mapped objects. |
| Change-source check | 1. |
| Writes to Salesforce | For each read-write mapping: changed rows ÷ 200, rounded up, per send. Each send is at least 1 call, and a mapping sends at most once per maximum wait (60 seconds by default) unless 200 changes are waiting. Runs of 2,000 or more go through Bulk API at about 6 calls each. |

One-off work, such as initial loads and Reloads, comes on top. A REST load costs about 1 call per 2,000 records. A Bulk load costs about 5 calls plus 1 per 50,000 records. AlgoBridge picks the cheaper one.

### Worked example

The figures below are arithmetic from stated assumptions, not measurements.

**Assumptions.** An Enterprise Edition org with 100 user licences, so the limit is 100,000 + 100 × 1,000 = **200,000 calls a day**. 50 mapped objects on the Composite probe. All 50 stay busy enough to poll at the 5-minute minimum all day (the worst case for detection). Each poll finds changes in 10 objects, each with fewer than 2,000 changed records. 5 of the mappings are read-write, and each sends one SOAP batch a minute, around the clock.

| Part | Arithmetic | Calls/day |
|---|---|---|
| Detection | 10 calls per poll × 288 polls | 2,880 |
| Fetch | 10 objects × 1 call × 288 polls | 2,880 |
| Sweep | 5 × 50 | 250 |
| Change-source check | | 1 |
| Writes to Salesforce | 5 mappings × 1,440 sends | 7,200 |
| **Total** | | **13,211** |

That is about 6.6% of the org's allowance, well under the 70% soft threshold.

Two changes would cut it sharply. Installing the [Apex bundle](../guides/apex-bundle.md) brings detection down from 2,880 to 288 calls. In practice, quiet objects back off toward the 30-minute maximum, so real detection and fetch costs are usually lower than this worst case.

!!! note "Your numbers"
    The connection screen shows the org's actual usage and AlgoBridge's share. After a day of real traffic, trust those figures over any estimate. See [Salesforce connection](../guides/salesforce-connection.md) and [Change sources](../guides/change-sources.md).

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/concepts/architecture/ -->
# Architecture

AlgoBridge is one container image. It talks to two PostgreSQL databases and one Salesforce org. It has no message broker, no cache and no shared disk. This page explains how those parts fit together and why the design is so small.

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/architecture.html?embed=1" title="AlgoBridge system architecture" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the architecture diagram full size](../assets/diagrams/architecture.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

## One instance, one sync pair

An instance syncs exactly one Salesforce org with exactly one client PostgreSQL database. There are no workspaces and no tenants. If you need to sync a second org or a second database, run a second instance.

This keeps the product easy to reason about. Every setting, every job and every alert on an instance belongs to the same pair, and you never have to ask which connection a row belongs to.

## One image, three roles

The same image runs in any of three roles. You choose the role with the `APP_ROLE` environment variable.

| `APP_ROLE` | Serves the console | Runs sync jobs | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `all` (default) | yes | yes | A single container. Good for most installs. |
| `web` | yes | no | Scale the console separately from the sync work. |
| `worker` | no | yes | Run sync work away from the public endpoint. |

A fourth mode applies the database migrations and exits. Run it with `docker run <image> migrate`, or set `MIGRATE_ON_BOOT=true` to have the container migrate before it starts. A `web` or `worker` process refuses to boot against a database whose schema is behind its build. It tells you to run the migration first instead of starting in a broken state.

Each process exposes `/healthz` (the process is alive) and `/readyz` (it can reach its database and is ready for traffic).

See [Workers and jobs](../guides/workers-and-jobs.md) for running several workers.

## All coordination happens in PostgreSQL

AlgoBridge has no Redis, no message broker and no external queue. Jobs, locks, schedules and the worker registry all live in PostgreSQL. The job engine keeps its tables in the `algobridge_jobs` schema of AlgoBridge's own database. No process holds coordination state in memory.

This has three practical results:

- **Nothing extra to run.** You operate PostgreSQL and a container. There is no second stateful service to back up, patch or monitor.
- **Workers are interchangeable.** Any worker can pick up any job. If a worker dies, another one takes over its work in about 20 seconds.
- **Restarts are safe.** On a normal stop, a worker finishes in-flight work for up to 30 seconds before it exits. Give your container runtime a stop grace period of 45 seconds so the drain can complete.

Each mapping runs on a short self-rescheduling tick of about 10 seconds. A watchdog checks every minute and restarts any mapping whose tick chain has broken. A tick that fails 5 times in a row is set aside as a dead job, so it cannot loop forever.

## Two databases, two owners

AlgoBridge uses two PostgreSQL databases. They must be different databases. They may share a server.

| | AlgoBridge's own database | Your client database |
|---|---|---|
| Owned by | AlgoBridge | You |
| Set by | `DATABASE_URL` | the console, or `CLIENT_DATABASE_URL` |
| Holds | users and sessions, the Salesforce connection, mappings, jobs and the worker registry, sync runs, alerts, idempotency keys, instance settings, poll watermarks, notifier keys | your mapped tables and the small set of objects AlgoBridge needs to capture your changes |
| Schema changes | migrations shipped with each release | only additive changes you approve in the console |

The split exists so that AlgoBridge's bookkeeping never mixes with your data. You can grant AlgoBridge narrow rights on your database, back the two up on different schedules, and remove AlgoBridge without leaving product tables among your own.

AlgoBridge enforces the split. It refuses to use its own database as the client database, and the migration refuses to run against a database that already holds AlgoBridge's change log. No transaction ever spans both databases.

### What AlgoBridge adds to your database

Everything AlgoBridge creates in your database lives in one schema, `algobridge` by default, and carries the `algobridge_` prefix. The prefix keeps its objects distinct from yours and from any other sync tool on the same database.

| Object | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Your mapped tables | One table per mapped Salesforce object, with a unique index on `sfid` and, where you choose one, on the External ID column. |
| `hstore` extension | Stores each captured change as old and new key-value pairs. |
| `algobridge_change_log` | The queue of changes waiting to go to Salesforce. |
| `algobridge_change_log_archive` | Sent changes, kept for 30 days for the Activity screen. |
| `algobridge_capture_change()` and the `algobridge_capture` trigger | Records every insert, update and delete on a read-write table. |
| `algobridge_lastop`, `algobridge_err`, `algobridge_id` columns | On read-write tables only: the row's last sync state, its last error, and a stable row identity. |

Read-only mappings get no trigger and no status columns.

!!! warning "Schema changes are additive only"
    AlgoBridge never drops or recreates one of your tables. It adds columns and indexes; it never narrows a column type. When you remove a field from a mapping, its column stays. Every change is shown to you as a diff and runs only when you press **Apply**. Before it runs, a preflight check names any database grant that is missing. See [Client database](../guides/client-database.md).

!!! note "TRUNCATE is not captured"
    Row triggers do not fire on `TRUNCATE`, so a truncated table is not synced to Salesforce. Use `DELETE` when you want removals to reach Salesforce.

## Runs anywhere a container runs

AlgoBridge is built to be provider-agnostic. It needs three things:

1. A long-lived container runtime.
2. PostgreSQL 15 or later.
3. Outbound HTTPS to Salesforce.

Beyond that it makes no assumptions about where it runs:

- Secrets arrive as environment variables.
- All state lives in PostgreSQL, so the container needs no local disk.
- Logs go to standard output.
- TLS ends at your reverse proxy or load balancer.
- Sign-in is local accounts or any OpenID Connect provider.
- Email, when you want it, is plain SMTP.
- The application code calls no cloud-provider SDK.

The image is built for more than one CPU architecture.

!!! tip "Scale-to-zero platforms"
    AlgoBridge runs scheduled work, so it must stay running. On a platform that scales idle containers to zero, set the minimum instance count to at least 1.

Next: [Salesforce to PostgreSQL](salesforce-to-postgres.md), or go straight to [Install](../getting-started/install.md).

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/concepts/change-notifier/ -->
# The change notifier

When a record is saved in Salesforce, a small Apex bundle tells your AlgoBridge instance which object changed. The instance then fetches the changed rows with one batched SOQL query and writes them to PostgreSQL. Learning about the change costs no Salesforce API calls, and an hourly fallback poll catches any notification that gets lost.

This page explains how that works. To set it up, follow [Install the Apex bundle](../guides/apex-bundle.md). To compare the notifier with polling, see [Change sources](../guides/change-sources.md).

<div class="ab-steps" markdown>

| When | Step | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Once | **Pair** | The operator clicks **Pair**. The org and the instance swap a signing key in 2 API calls. |
| Once per object | **Add Flows** | A save Flow and a delete Flow are added for each notified object. |
| Every save | **Notify** | The Flow queues a signed POST that carries object names only. This costs 0 API calls. |
| Per burst of notifications | **Fetch** | One SOQL fetch per mapping pulls every row changed since the watermark into PostgreSQL. |

</div>

## System map

The left region is what gets installed in your org. The right region is the AlgoBridge container behind its TLS proxy. Bold lines are the path a save takes. Red lines carry a signature or a certificate. Dashed lines are reads or one-off setup.

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe class="tall" src="../../assets/diagrams/notifier/system-map.html?embed=1" title="Change notifier system map" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the system map full size](../assets/diagrams/notifier/system-map.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

## What gets installed in your org

You deploy the bundle once from the **Connections** screen. Every name in it starts with `algobridge_`, so nothing in it can collide with anything else in your org.

| Resource | Kind | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `algobridge_Status` | Apex REST | Reports the bundle version, whether the org is paired, the endpoint, and who paired it. The console calls it after pairing and in the daily check. |
| `algobridge_ChangeProbe` | Apex REST | Answers one question for many objects in a single call: has anything changed since this time? The fallback poll uses it, so 50 objects cost 1 call, not 50. |
| `algobridge_NotifierPair` | Apex REST | Takes the one-time pairing code from the console, redeems it with the instance, and stores the key it receives. |
| `algobridge_NotifyChange` | Invocable action | Called by the Flows. It removes duplicate object names, skips saves it should not report, checks the async limits, and queues the send. It catches every error, so it can never fail a user's save. |
| `algobridge_Notifier` | `@future` callout | Signs the list of object names and posts it to the instance. It uses a 10-second timeout, never retries, never follows redirects, and presents a client certificate when one is configured. |
| `algobridge_Notifier__c` | Custom setting (hierarchy) | Holds the instance endpoint, key id, signing secret, org id, the pairing user and an optional client certificate name. Only `NotifierPair` writes it. |
| `algobridge_Integration` | Permission set | Grants the classes to the integration user that AlgoBridge connects as. |
| `algobridge_Instance` | Remote site setting | Lets Apex call your instance's HTTPS host. It is set to your instance URL at deploy time. |

Each Apex class ships with its own test class.

For every synced object, two record-triggered Flows call `NotifyChange`:

| Flow | Runs | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `algobridge_notify_<object>_<hash>_save` | After save | Fires on create and update. |
| `algobridge_notify_<object>_<hash>_delete` | Before delete | Fires on delete. It has to run before the delete, because the record no longer exists afterwards. |

The hash is six characters derived from the object's API name. It keeps long names unique within Salesforce's 80-character limit for Flow names.

!!! note "Adding the Flows"
    Today you add the Flows by hand, following the recipe in [Install the Apex bundle](../guides/apex-bundle.md). A coming release adds a background job that deploys and removes them for you. It is described [below](#planned-the-flows-job).

## Pairing: one click, two calls

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/notifier/pairing.html?embed=1" title="Pairing sequence" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the pairing sequence full size](../assets/diagrams/notifier/pairing.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

1. **The console opens a pairing slot.** Clicking **Pair** writes a one-time code to AlgoBridge's database. If the round trip hasn't finished within 3 minutes, the code stops working.
2. **The console calls the org once.** It sends `POST /services/apexrest/algobridge/v1/notifier/pair` with the code and the instance's notify URL, plus the client certificate name when mutual TLS is on. This is the first of the two Salesforce calls.
3. **Apex calls the instance back.** `NotifierPair` sends `{code, orgId, apexVersion}` to `/notify/v1/pair`. The instance redeems the code once, generates a key, encrypts the secret with AES-GCM, pins the key to the org id, and returns `{keyId, secret, notifyUrl}`.
4. **Apex stores the key and answers.** The key goes into `algobridge_Notifier__c` with the user who paired. The console receives `{paired, keyId, pairedBy}`, and one status call confirms it. That is the second Salesforce call.

!!! tip "Why the org calls the instance"
    The secret never passes through your browser or clipboard, and the instance learns the org id from the org itself. Pairing again rotates the key, and the old key stops working straight away.

## A record save, end to end

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/notifier/save-to-postgres.html?embed=1" title="From a record save to PostgreSQL" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the save sequence full size](../assets/diagrams/notifier/save-to-postgres.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

1. **The Flow fires inside the user's transaction.** The save Flow or the delete Flow calls `algobridge_NotifyChange.notify`, passing only the object name. Record data never leaves the org on this path.
2. **`NotifyChange` decides whether to send.** It skips the send when:
    - the save came from the integration user. That is AlgoBridge writing PostgreSQL changes back, and reporting it would echo the change.
    - the org isn't paired.
    - the code is already running in a future or batch context, where Salesforce doesn't allow another `@future` call.
    - the transaction has used up its future-call limit.
    - the org is within the last 1% of its daily async Apex allowance. That last 1% is left for your own automation.

    Otherwise it queues one `@future` call per transaction, carrying the object names with duplicates removed. It catches every exception, so the save always commits.
3. **`Notifier` signs and posts after the commit.** The callout builds the body and signs it with HMAC-SHA256 over a canonical string. The request has a 10-second timeout and is never retried or redirected.
4. **The instance checks the request, cheapest check first.** The first check that fails rejects the request, so the expensive checks run only once the cheap ones have passed.
5. **One fetch per mapping.** For each mapping on a named object, the instance queues one `sf-fetch` job and answers `{accepted, ignored}`. Only one fetch job per mapping can be waiting at a time. A bulk load of 10,000 records sends many notifications, but they collapse into a single fetch.
6. **SOQL since the watermark, then upsert.** The fetch runs under the [API budget governor](api-budget.md). It reads every row changed since the mapping's watermark in REST query pages, and applies them 500 rows at a time. It upserts the rows into your PostgreSQL by `sfid`, then moves the watermark forward.

=== "Signed request"

    ```http
    POST /notify/v1/changes
    AlgoBridge-Key-Id:    <key id>
    AlgoBridge-Org:       <18-character org id>
    AlgoBridge-Timestamp: <unix seconds>
    AlgoBridge-Nonce:     <random>
    AlgoBridge-Signature: v1=<hex>

    {"v":1,"objects":["Account","Contact"]}
    ```

=== "What the signature covers"

    ```text
    v1
    POST
    /notify/v1/changes
    <timestamp>
    <nonce>
    <org id>
    <sha256(body) hex>

    signature = hex(HMAC-SHA256(secret, string))
    ```

### The checks on `/notify/v1/changes`

| Order | Check | What it stops |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | The body is at most 16 KB and is valid JSON | Oversized or garbage payloads, before any lookup |
| 2 | The key id is known and active | Strangers and rotated keys |
| 3 | The timestamp is within 5 minutes of the instance's clock | Captured requests replayed later |
| 4 | The signature matches, compared in constant time | Forged or altered requests, and timing probes |
| 5 | The org header matches the key's org and the connected org | A key copied into another org |
| 6 | The nonce hasn't been seen in the last 10 minutes | Replays inside the time window |
| 7 | The body lists 1 to 200 object names | Malformed bodies |
| 8 | At most 60 requests a minute per key | Floods from a misbehaving org |

## Safety nets

A notification is a hint to fetch now, not the data itself. If one is lost, the sync is delayed but never wrong, because each of these nets catches up on its own.

| What happens | What catches it | Cost |
|---|---|---:|
| The instance is down, or a callout times out | The **hourly fallback poll**. It runs on the hour, so all notified mappings share one `ChangeProbe` call and fetch only the objects that changed. The interval is `sf_notifier_fallback_seconds`, 3600 by default. | 1 call an hour |
| An admin deactivates or deletes one of the Flows | The **daily check**: one status call and one Flow listing. Drift shows on the mapping's chip. AlgoBridge never turns a Flow back on against an admin's decision. | 2 calls a day |
| The key is rotated, or the org is paired somewhere else | Requests signed with the old key fail check 2 and are refused. The fallback poll keeps data flowing until the org is paired again. | 0 |
| The org is close to its daily async Apex allowance | `NotifyChange` stops queueing at the 1% reserve, and the fallback poll takes over. | 0 |
| A delete or an edit slips past everything | The nightly reconciliation sweep compares ids and catches it. | Already budgeted |

## What change detection costs

AlgoBridge counts against your org's daily API limit, so every way of detecting changes has a price in calls per day. These figures are for **50 synced objects**. Fetching the changed rows costs the same whichever way a change was detected, so it isn't included.

| Detection | How | Calls a day |
|---|---|---:|
| Composite polling | Ask every object for changes on the adaptive interval | about 480 to 7,200 |
| Apex probe polling | One `ChangeProbe` call covers all 50 objects | about 48 to 720 |
| **Notifier** | Saves push object names, plus the hourly fallback probe and the daily check | **0 + 24 + 2** |
| One-off setup | Pairing (2 calls), and the Flow deploy once the Flows job ships (at most 8 per object) | up to 402, once |

## Planned: the Flows job

!!! info "Coming in a later release"
    This section describes behaviour that is still being built. It may change before release.

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/notifier/flows-job.html?embed=1" title="The Flows job" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the Flows job diagram full size](../assets/diagrams/notifier/flows-job.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

Whenever a mapping is turned on or off, or the notifier is paired, a background job runs for each affected object. Only one job runs per object at a time, so two triggers for the same object never race. Each run:

1. **Plans.** It lists the object's existing Flows (1 call). It wants a Flow pair if the mapping is on, and nothing if it is off.
2. **Retires a hand-made Flow.** It deactivates any Flow added by hand from the recipe, so the object doesn't notify twice (up to 2 calls).
3. **Deploys or removes the pair.** It makes one Metadata API deploy and polls it about 3 times. When the mapping is off, the same step removes the Flows and the chip reads **removed**.
4. **Reads back and activates.** It reads what was deployed (1 call) and switches on any of its Flows that are still inactive (up to 2 calls). If the org refuses, the chip reads **inactive · activate in Setup** and the job doesn't fail.

That is at most 8 calls per object, spent once. For 50 objects that is at most 400 calls, and the governor spreads them out. While the governor has paused spending, the job waits and runs later. A configuration problem, such as a missing permission, marks the job failed without retrying. A temporary failure retries. Either way, the mapping keeps syncing on the hourly fallback poll.

## Planned: hardening the notify endpoint

Two optional layers are planned for locked-down deployments. Both sit on top of the request signature, and neither replaces it.

Mutual TLS
:   You upload a client certificate to Salesforce and name it during pairing. The `Notifier` presents it on every send. Your reverse proxy verifies the certificate and forwards its fingerprint in a header. AlgoBridge trusts that header only on requests that come from an address in `TRUSTED_PROXIES`, so a client can't forge it by sending the header itself.

Source allow-list
:   You choose a verified source: a list of Salesforce egress address ranges. AlgoBridge refuses requests from any other address.

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/concepts/conflicts/ -->
# Conflicts

A conflict happens when the same record changes in Salesforce and in PostgreSQL before either change has reached the other side. This page explains exactly when AlgoBridge treats a change as a conflict, and the three policies you can choose for resolving one.

Conflicts only arise on **read-write** mappings. A read-only mapping never writes to Salesforce, so its table simply follows Salesforce.

## When is it a conflict?

"Both sides changed" has a narrow and exact meaning in AlgoBridge. A conflict exists only while the change log holds an **unsent** PostgreSQL change for the record, that is, a change still in the `NEW` or `CLAIMED` state, at the moment a Salesforce change for the same record arrives.

Anything else is not a conflict:

- A PostgreSQL change that has already been sent and accepted is settled. A later Salesforce change is simply applied.
- A Salesforce change that has already been applied is settled. A later PostgreSQL change is simply sent.

AlgoBridge makes the decision inside the inbound apply transaction, after it has locked the affected rows. An edit you commit while the batch is waiting for its locks is still seen. An edit that comes after waits for the batch to finish. So there is no window in which a change slips past the check.

## The three policies

You set the policy per mapping in the mapping editor. A read-write mapping must have one; the editor defaults to `sf_wins`.

| Policy | What the incoming Salesforce change does | What the pending PostgreSQL change does |
|---|---|---|
| `sf_wins` (default) | Applied to your row. | Still sent afterwards. |
| `pg_wins` | Skipped this pass. Your row is left exactly as it is. | Sent as normal. |
| `latest_wins` | Applied if Salesforce's change is the same age or newer; skipped if it is older. | Sent as normal. |

The policy only decides what happens to the incoming Salesforce change. It never cancels a pending PostgreSQL change.

### `sf_wins`

Salesforce's version of the record is written to your table at once. Your pending change is still sent afterwards. Updates send only the fields you changed, so Salesforce ends up holding your values for those fields, and its own values everywhere else. The next poll brings that combined record back to PostgreSQL.

Choose this when PostgreSQL should always reflect Salesforce as soon as possible, and your own edits are expected to go through.

### `pg_wins`

The incoming Salesforce change is skipped for this pass, and your row keeps your edit. The watermark still moves past the record, so AlgoBridge does not read it again and again. Your change is then sent. That send gives the record a new `SystemModstamp`, so the next poll fetches it and brings back the combined record.

Choose this when PostgreSQL is the system where edits matter most, and you never want an incoming change to overwrite a row with a send still pending.

### `latest_wins`

AlgoBridge compares two timestamps:

- the record's `SystemModstamp` in Salesforce, and
- the time your newest unsent change to the record was captured in PostgreSQL.

If the Salesforce change is newer, it is applied as with `sf_wins`. If your change is newer, the Salesforce change is skipped as with `pg_wins`. **Ties go to Salesforce.** Salesforce timestamps are accurate only to the second, and re-applying a record costs nothing, while dropping one could lose an edit.

!!! note "Clock accuracy"
    `latest_wins` compares a timestamp taken by Salesforce with one taken by your database, so it is only as good as your database server's clock. `sf_wins` and `pg_wins` do not depend on clocks at all.

## Loads and the sweep always side with Salesforce

The conflict policy applies to day-to-day polling. Two jobs follow fixed rules instead:

- **Reload** empties the table and loads it again from Salesforce.
- The **daily reconciliation sweep** overwrites rows that differ from Salesforce with Salesforce's values. It skips any row that still has a change waiting to be sent. That pending change then goes out and settles the record in the normal way.

See [Salesforce to PostgreSQL](salesforce-to-postgres.md#initial-load-reload-and-the-daily-sweep) for both.

## Why a policy matters

Many sync tools have no conflict setting and simply call their sync eventually consistent, so which edit survives is left to timing. AlgoBridge offers the three policies above per mapping, and the default, `sf_wins`, gives a predictable result for most installs.

See [Mappings](../guides/mappings.md) to set a mapping's policy.

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/concepts/postgres-to-salesforce/ -->
# PostgreSQL to Salesforce

This page explains how a row you insert, update or delete in PostgreSQL reaches Salesforce. It applies to mappings set to **read-write**. Read-only mappings never write to Salesforce.

The path has four steps:

1. **Capture.** A trigger on your table records the change in a log, inside your own transaction.
2. **Batch.** Changes wait briefly so they can be sent together.
3. **Send.** A batch goes to Salesforce over SOAP or Bulk API v2, whichever costs fewer calls.
4. **Write back.** Salesforce's answer, including the new record Id, is written to your row.

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/postgres-to-salesforce.html?embed=1" title="PostgreSQL to Salesforce data flow" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the PostgreSQL to Salesforce data flow full size](../assets/diagrams/postgres-to-salesforce.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

## Capture: a trigger and a change log

When you activate a read-write mapping, AlgoBridge adds a trigger named `algobridge_capture` to its table. The trigger runs before every insert, update and delete, for each row. It writes the row's old and new values, as `hstore`, to `algobridge_change_log`, and it sets the row's `algobridge_lastop` column to `PENDING`.

Because the trigger runs inside your transaction, capture is exact. A change is logged only if your transaction commits, and a rollback leaves nothing behind. Your application keeps writing plain SQL. It needs no client library and makes no API call.

Capture never stops. Even when the [API budget governor](api-budget.md#the-governor) pauses sending, the trigger keeps logging, so nothing is lost while Salesforce is out of reach.

!!! warning "What the trigger cannot see"
    A trigger captures only the writes that fire it. Three things bypass it, and changes made that way never reach Salesforce:

    - `TRUNCATE`, which fires no row trigger. Use `DELETE` when you want removals to reach Salesforce.
    - Disabling the trigger with `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER`.
    - A session with `session_replication_role = replica`, which skips ordinary triggers.

## Batching: size and maximum wait

Sending one change per API call would quickly exhaust your org's limits. So AlgoBridge waits for changes to accumulate, within a bound you control.

Every mapping checks its queue on a tick of about 10 seconds. The check reads PostgreSQL only and costs no Salesforce call. A send starts when either of these is true:

- **200 changes are waiting.** That fills one SOAP call.
- **The oldest change has waited longer than the maximum wait.** The default is 60 seconds, adjustable from 10 to 900 seconds with `outbound_max_wait_seconds`.

So a busy table sends full batches quickly, and a quiet table sends a single change within about a minute. While the governor has slowed the instance, the maximum wait is multiplied by 4.

A send claims up to 10,000 waiting changes at once. Claims use `SKIP LOCKED`, so two workers never take the same row. Within a mapping, changes are claimed strictly in capture order.

## Choosing the transport: SOAP or Bulk API v2

AlgoBridge picks the transport by estimated call cost.

| | SOAP | Bulk API v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Records per call | up to 200 | a job, any size |
| Cost | 1 call per 200 records | about 6 calls per job |
| Used when | runs under 2,000 records, and always for Merged writes | runs of 2,000 or more of the same action, Ordered writes only |
| Answers | at once | asynchronously |

A Bulk job's fixed overhead makes it more expensive than SOAP below about 1,200 records. Switching at 2,000 leaves a clear margin. A Bulk insert also needs the mapping's External ID field so results can be matched back to rows. Without one, the run simply stays on SOAP.

Updates send only the fields that changed. A field you set to `NULL` is sent as a cleared field. Inserts send every writable field.

### Ordered and Merged writes

The instance's write algorithm controls how several changes to the same record are sent.

| | Ordered (default) | Merged |
|---|---|---|
| Several changes to one record | Sent one by one, in order | Folded before sending: an insert plus updates becomes one insert, several updates become one update with the latest values |
| Transport | SOAP, or Bulk for large runs | SOAP only |

Ordered is the safe choice for most installs. Merged saves calls when the same records are updated many times between sends.

### Parents before children

If a row refers to a parent record that has not reached Salesforce yet, the row is held back until the parent is inserted. Only that record and its children wait; everything else keeps syncing, where some sync tools stop the whole queue behind one failed insert.

## Write-back and echo suppression

The Salesforce call runs between two short database transactions, so no lock on your table is held while AlgoBridge waits on the network.

When Salesforce answers, AlgoBridge writes back to each row: the new `sfid` for an insert, the system fields, and the sync state in `algobridge_lastop` and `algobridge_err`. The sent changes move to `algobridge_change_log_archive` in the same transaction. They stay there for 30 days for the Activity screen.

The write-back runs under `SET LOCAL ab.in_sync = true`. The capture trigger sees that setting and does not log these writes. Without it, writing the `sfid` back would itself look like a new change and be sent again. The setting is local to the transaction, so your own sessions are never affected.

## When Salesforce says no

Each change in the log has a state.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `NEW` | Waiting to be sent. |
| `CLAIMED` | Taken by a send in progress. |
| `DONE` | Accepted by Salesforce. |
| `MERGED` | Folded into another change by Merged writes. |
| `DEAD` | Failed for good; needs your decision. |
| `DISCARDED` | You chose to drop it. |

### Transient failures are retried

A rejection from Salesforce is always retried, because it is often temporary: a locked record, a validation rule someone is about to fix, or a missing parent. Each change gets 5 attempts. The delay grows from 60 seconds and doubles each time, capped at one hour, with random jitter so retries do not arrive in step. A change that keeps failing reaches `DEAD` after about 15 minutes.

If a worker stops in the middle of a send, its claimed changes return to `NEW` after 21 minutes and are sent again. Inserts go as upserts on the External ID where the mapping has one, so a resent insert updates the record the first attempt created instead of making a duplicate.

### Permanent failures stop at once

Some changes can never be sent, whatever Salesforce says. An example is a row whose value cannot be converted to the field's type. AlgoBridge marks these `DEAD` straight away rather than wasting calls on retries.

### Dead changes stay visible

A `DEAD` change stays in the live log. It is not silently dropped. On the Activity screen you can retry or discard one change, or retry every failed change at once.

!!! info "Error text never reaches the logs"
    Salesforce's error messages can quote the field values you sent. AlgoBridge stores the error with the change and shows it only on the Activity screen, behind sign-in. It never writes it to a log line.

See [Mappings](../guides/mappings.md) to make a mapping read-write, and [Live log](../guides/live-log.md) to watch sends as they happen.

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/concepts/salesforce-to-postgres/ -->
# Salesforce to PostgreSQL

This page explains how a change made in Salesforce reaches your PostgreSQL table. Each mapped object goes through the same three steps:

1. **Detect.** Find out cheaply whether the object has changed since the last pass.
2. **Fetch.** Read only the changed records, in large pages.
3. **Apply.** Write them to your table in one transaction, matched on `sfid`.

AlgoBridge detects changes by polling with SOQL, or by being told about them by the optional [change notifier](change-notifier.md). It does not use Salesforce Change Data Capture or streaming events.

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/salesforce-to-postgres.html?embed=1" title="Salesforce to PostgreSQL sequence" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the Salesforce to PostgreSQL sequence full size](../assets/diagrams/salesforce-to-postgres.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

## Why polling, and why it is cheap

Every call AlgoBridge makes counts against your org's daily API limit (see [API budget](api-budget.md)). So the design goal is simple: never spend a call per record, and spend as few calls as possible when nothing has changed. In most orgs, most objects are unchanged most of the time. A cheap "has anything changed?" check, followed by a full read only when the answer is yes, uses far fewer calls than reading every object on a timer.

## Watermarks

AlgoBridge keeps a watermark for each mapping in its own database. The watermark is the `SystemModstamp` of the newest record it has applied. Every detect and fetch asks for records at or after that stamp.

The watermark is deliberately cautious:

- **It only moves after the apply commits.** It advances to the highest stamp actually written to your table. A crash mid-fetch repeats some work; it never skips a record.
- **It uses `>=`, not `>`.** SOQL timestamps have one-second resolution, so several records can share a stamp. Re-reading the boundary second is cheap and safe, because the apply is idempotent.
- **It stays 120 seconds behind the present.** A record saved in a long Salesforce transaction can appear with a stamp slightly in the past. Holding the watermark back by two minutes keeps such records from being missed.
- **A long gap triggers a full fetch.** If a watermark is more than 14 days old, AlgoBridge treats the mapping as out of date and fetches it in full. Salesforce keeps deleted records in the recycle bin for 15 days, so a shorter gap still sees every deletion.

## Detecting changes: probes

A probe asks one question per object: has any record changed since the watermark? A singleton probe job runs once a minute and checks every mapping that is due. You choose how the probe is answered. This choice is the instance's **change source**.

| Change source | How it asks | Objects per call | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Composite** (default) | One `queryAll` of `SELECT Id … WHERE SystemModstamp >= <watermark> LIMIT 1` per object, bundled into one Composite request | 5 | nothing extra |
| **Apex probe** | One call to the AlgoBridge Apex class, which runs the same check for each object inside Salesforce | 90 | the [Apex bundle](../guides/apex-bundle.md) installed in the org |
| **Change notifier** | Salesforce posts the names of changed objects to AlgoBridge | 0 per change | the Apex bundle, Flows on each object, and a reachable AlgoBridge URL |

The Composite probe uses `queryAll` so that deleted records count as changes too.

The Apex probe class is read-only. It runs `with sharing` and in user mode, so it sees only what the integration user may see. It never returns record data, only which objects have changed.

### Choosing and keeping a change source

You pick the change source on the console. AlgoBridge checks that the source works, with one status call, before it saves your choice. After that it re-checks once a day at 02:20 UTC, at a cost of 1 call.

If your chosen source stops working, for example because someone removed the Apex class, AlgoBridge falls back to the next one that still works. The notifier falls back to the Apex probe if it is verified, and otherwise to Composite. At the same time it opens an alert. Your selection is never changed for you. Once you fix the cause, the next check restores your chosen source. See [Change sources](../guides/change-sources.md).

### The change notifier, in short

With the notifier, two record-triggered Flows on each object call an Apex action when a record is saved. The action sends AlgoBridge one signed `POST /notify/v1/changes` naming the objects that changed. It never sends record data. Salesforce's outbound callouts do not count as API requests, so detection costs nothing per change. AlgoBridge then fetches the changes as usual.

The notifier is a fast path, not the only path. Flows do not fire in every case (undelete and merge, for example). A slow fallback poll, hourly by default, and the daily sweep catch anything a notification missed. The [Change notifier](change-notifier.md) page covers pairing, the request checks, the safety nets and the costs in full.

## Adaptive intervals

Each mapping has its own probe interval, and AlgoBridge adjusts it to how busy the object is:

- It starts at the **minimum interval**: 300 seconds by default, adjustable from 120 to 3600 seconds.
- After 3 empty probes in a row, the interval doubles, up to the **maximum interval** (1800 seconds by default).
- As soon as a probe finds a change, the interval drops back to the minimum.
- If Salesforce rejects one object's probe, only that mapping backs off. The others in the same call carry on.

A busy object is checked often. A quiet one costs a few calls an hour. When the [API budget governor](api-budget.md#the-governor) slows the instance down, all intervals stretch further.

## Fetching changed records

When a probe reports a change, AlgoBridge reads the changed records with one `queryAll`. The query selects the mapped fields plus `IsDeleted`, ordered by `SystemModstamp` ascending. Salesforce returns up to 2,000 records per page, and each page is one API call. Records are applied in batches of 500.

Formula fields are never synced. Their values change without changing `SystemModstamp`, so polling could never keep them correct. Leaving them out is more honest than syncing values that silently go stale.

## Applying records: upsert on `sfid`

Each batch is applied to your table in one transaction:

1. **Deletes first.** Records Salesforce reports as deleted are removed by `sfid`.
2. **Match on External ID.** If the mapping has an External ID field, a row with the same External ID and no `sfid` yet is updated and gains its `sfid`. This links rows you inserted in PostgreSQL before Salesforce assigned an Id.
3. **Upsert on `sfid`.** Every live record is then inserted, or updated where a row with the same Salesforce Id already exists.

If one row cannot be written, for example because a value breaks one of your constraints, that row is skipped and counted. The rest of the batch still commits. One bad row never blocks a whole object.

### Echo suppression

The apply runs under `SET LOCAL ab.in_sync = true`. The capture trigger on your table sees that setting and does not record these writes as new changes. Without it, every record AlgoBridge pulled from Salesforce would be sent straight back. The setting is local to the transaction, so it can never leak into your own sessions.

When a record has also changed on the PostgreSQL side, the apply follows the mapping's [conflict policy](conflicts.md).

## Initial load, reload and the daily sweep

Polling handles day-to-day changes. Three other jobs keep a table complete:

- **Initial load.** When you activate a mapping, AlgoBridge counts the records and loads them all. It picks whichever transport costs fewer calls: REST queries at about one call per 2,000 records, or a Bulk API query at about 5 calls plus one per 50,000 records. When the load ends, the watermark is set to the moment it started, so changes made during the load are picked up next.
- **Reload.** Empties the table and loads it again from Salesforce. Because it erases data, you confirm it by typing the table name.
- **Daily reconciliation sweep.** Once a day, by default at 03:00 UTC, one Bulk query reads every mapped field of every record, at about 5 calls per mapping. The sweep removes rows Salesforce no longer has and fixes rows that differ, with Salesforce's value winning. It catches what polling cannot, such as records purged from the recycle bin before a poll saw them. It skips rows with a change still waiting to go out, and it refuses to delete a large share of a table at once. It waits while the [governor](api-budget.md#the-governor) has slowed or paused the instance.

See [Mappings](../guides/mappings.md) for activating, reloading and sweeping a mapping, and [Live log](../guides/live-log.md) to watch these passes as they run.

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/concepts/security/ -->
# Security

AlgoBridge holds credentials for your Salesforce org and your database, and it can change records in both. This page explains how it protects them: who can sign in, what each role can do, how every change is protected against forgery and double submission, how stored secrets are encrypted, and what data leaves your network.

## Sign-in

AlgoBridge supports two ways to sign in. You can use both at once.

**Local accounts.** Email and password, with optional two-step verification (TOTP). Passwords are hashed with argon2id. The first administrator is created from the command line with `create-admin`. Local accounts also serve as a break-glass route if your identity provider is unavailable.

**Single sign-on.** One OpenID Connect adapter, with presets for Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID, and a generic option for any other OIDC provider. Several providers can be active at the same time. See [Single sign-on](../guides/sso.md).

A few rules apply to every sign-in:

- **Identities are keyed by issuer and subject, never by email.** Changing an email address at your provider cannot hand an account to someone else.
- **Invite-only by default.** A person needs an invitation before they can sign in. To allow self sign-up through single sign-on, list your email domains in `AUTH_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`. A person with a verified email in one of those domains is created on first sign-in, as a viewer.
- **You decide who may use a password.** `AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN` is `all` (the default), `admins` (only administrators may sign in with a password) or `off` (single sign-on only).

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Session lifetime | 12 hours, absolute |
| Idle timeout | 2 hours |
| Failed attempts before lockout | 5 |
| Lockout | 15 minutes |
| Invite and password-reset links | single use, valid for 7 days |
| A started SSO sign-in | must finish within 10 minutes |

## Roles

AlgoBridge has three roles. Permissions are defined in code, not edited in the console, so a role means the same thing on every instance.

| Role | Can |
|---|---|
| **Viewer** | See sync status and errors. |
| **Member** | Everything a viewer can, plus retry failed records, operate sync, and create, edit and delete mappings. |
| **Admin** | Everything, including managing connections, users and settings, and viewing the [Live log](../guides/live-log.md). |

Every route is denied unless it names the permission it needs, so a new screen cannot ship open by accident. AlgoBridge also refuses to remove or demote the last administrator. See [Users and roles](../guides/users-and-roles.md).

## Every write is forgery-checked and idempotent

Every form that changes something carries two hidden values:

- **A signed form token** (`_csrf`) proves the form came from AlgoBridge, for this session. The token is an HMAC-SHA256 signature, using a key stored in AlgoBridge's database, and it is bound to your session. A forged or missing token is refused. Scripts send it in the `Algobridge-Form-Token` header.
- **A one-time idempotency key** (`_idem`) is issued fresh each time a form is shown. If the same form is submitted twice, for example by a double click or a browser retry, the action runs once.

How a repeated submission is answered:

| Case | Answer |
|---|---|
| The first submission redirected | The same redirect is sent again. Nothing runs twice. |
| The first submission rendered a page | `409`. A rendered page may show a one-time secret, so it is never replayed. |
| The first submission is still running | `409`. |
| Same key, different form contents | `422`. |

Idempotency keys expire after 24 hours.

!!! warning "Serve AlgoBridge over HTTPS"
    Over HTTPS, AlgoBridge's cookies carry the `__Host-` prefix, which locks them to your exact origin. AlgoBridge refuses to start with a plain `http://` `PUBLIC_URL`, unless the URL is on loopback or you set `ALLOW_INSECURE_PUBLIC_URL=true`. Use that setting only for local testing.

## Encryption of stored secrets

Secrets AlgoBridge stores in its database are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under the key in `ENCRYPTION_KEY` (32 bytes, base64). This covers:

- the client database connection string,
- the Salesforce tokens and connected app secret,
- the change notifier's secrets,
- two-step verification keys.

Each value records which key encrypted it, so AlgoBridge can tell old keys from new.

### Rotating the key

1. Set the new key in `ENCRYPTION_KEY` and the old one in `ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS`.
2. Run the `rotate-encryption-key` command. It re-encrypts every stored secret under the new key in one transaction.
3. Remove `ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS`.

See [Configuration](../getting-started/configuration.md).

!!! danger "Keep the key safe"
    Without `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, the stored secrets cannot be decrypted. Store it in your secret manager or platform configuration, never in the image or in source control.

## The Salesforce connection

AlgoBridge connects to Salesforce through an External Client App that you create in your org, using OAuth with PKCE. It connects only to your org's My Domain (`*.my.salesforce.com`). Disconnecting revokes the token in Salesforce. Use a dedicated integration user, so you control exactly what AlgoBridge can see and change. See [Salesforce connection](../guides/salesforce-connection.md).

## Notifier request signing

When you use the [change notifier](change-notifier.md), Salesforce sends requests to AlgoBridge. Every request is signed with HMAC-SHA256 under a secret shared at pairing. AlgoBridge checks the key, the signature, the org, a timestamp within five minutes and a nonce it has not seen before. It also limits body size, the number of object names and the request rate. A refused request gets an empty answer, so a caller learns nothing about why it failed. Repeated refusals open an alert.

A notification carries only object API names, never record data. The worst a stolen secret allows is triggering early fetches, which the governor still bounds. The [Change notifier](change-notifier.md) page lists every check and covers key rotation and revocation.

## What data leaves your network

| Traffic | Direction | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| Salesforce API calls | outbound HTTPS | Queries and writes for the objects and fields you map. |
| Change notifications | inbound, from your Salesforce org | Object API names only, and only if you use the notifier. |
| Email | outbound SMTP | Invitation and password-reset links, and only if you configure SMTP. Without SMTP, the links are shown to the administrator instead. |

Nothing else leaves today. The current release has no telemetry and makes no calls to its maintainers.

Registration keys add no traffic. The instance checks its key itself, against public keys built into the image; to keep a key current you paste a status token from CloudAlgo into the License panel. A daily automatic check-in is planned for a later release. It will send the key, a random instance id, the AlgoBridge and Apex bundle versions, the org id (or, for the shared sandbox and Developer Edition keys, a one-way keyed hash of it) and a usage summary of counts, never names, emails, record data, object or field names, or credentials, and it will not be switched on before it is documented. See [Pricing](/pricing/#registration-keys).

Logs go to standard output and never carry field values or Salesforce error text. Salesforce error messages can quote the values you sent, so they are stored with the change and shown only on the authenticated Activity screen.

## Not yet built

These features are planned and are not in the current build:

- mutual TLS and an IP allow-list for the notifier endpoint.

The audit log of console actions, the `/api/v1` API with its access tokens, and outgoing webhooks are built; see [Release notes](../release-notes.md).

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/getting-started/configuration/ -->
# Configuration reference

This page lists every environment variable AlgoBridge reads, with its default and what it does. Use it when you write your Compose file, Kubernetes manifest or platform config.

AlgoBridge reads its configuration only from environment variables. It never calls a secrets-manager API: if your secrets live in one, have your platform inject them as environment variables.

## How configuration is checked

All settings are parsed once at start, against one schema. If anything is wrong, the process exits before it serves a request, with one line that names every problem:

```text
Invalid configuration — DATABASE_URL: must be a postgres:// connection string; SMTP_URL and SMTP_FROM must be set together
```

A few rules apply throughout:

- **An empty value counts as unset** for every optional variable, so `SMTP_URL=` is the same as leaving it out.
- **Lists are comma-separated.** Spaces around items are trimmed, items are lowercased, and duplicates are dropped.
- **Some variables come in sets.** Setting only part of a set, such as `SMTP_URL` without `SMTP_FROM`, is refused.
- **Set the same environment on every container.** Web and worker containers read the same variables, and the `migrate`, `create-admin` and `rotate-encryption-key` commands read them too.

## Core

| Variable | Default | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `APP_ROLE` | `all` | No | What the container runs: `all` (console and jobs), `web` (console only) or `worker` (jobs only). See [APP_ROLE](install.md#choose-an-app_role). |
| `PORT` | `3000` | No | The HTTP port every role listens on, including `worker`, for its health checks. An integer from 1 to 65535. |
| `PUBLIC_URL` | `http://localhost:3000` | Yes, outside a local trial | The address people reach the console at, such as `https://sync.example.com`. Must be a bare `http(s)` origin with no path, query or fragment. Must be `https://` unless the host is `localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`. Sign-in redirects, the Salesforce callback and the change notifier's endpoint are built from it, and requests from other origins are rejected. |
| `ALLOW_INSECURE_PUBLIC_URL` | unset | No | `true` accepts a plain `http://` `PUBLIC_URL` on a non-local host, for example on an isolated network. Session cookies can only be locked to the host over `https`, so use this only on a network you trust. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | No | The lowest level written to stdout: `fatal`, `error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug` or `trace`. Opening the [Live log](../guides/live-log.md) raises it to `debug` for the Live log only, never for stdout. |
| `MIGRATE_ON_BOOT` | unset | No | `true` makes the container's `serve` command run the platform database migrations before it starts the app. Read by the image's entrypoint, not by the app. Convenient for a single container; with several containers, run `migrate` as a separate step. |
| `BUILD_COMMIT` | set at build time | No | The git commit the image was built from, shown shortened in the sidebar footer. A 7 to 40 character hex SHA. Normally passed as the `BUILD_COMMIT` build argument rather than set at run time. |

The image also sets `NODE_ENV=production`. You don't need to change it.

## Databases

| Variable | Default | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | none | **Yes** | The platform database: AlgoBridge's own users, connections, mappings, jobs and sync state. A `postgres://` or `postgresql://` URL. PostgreSQL 15 or later. |
| `CLIENT_DATABASE_URL` | unset | No | The client database, the one AlgoBridge syncs. When set, it wins over a connection saved on the Connections screen, and the screen refuses to save or disconnect. See below for the format. |

`CLIENT_DATABASE_URL` is checked at start with the same rules the Connections screen uses. It must:

- start with `postgres://` or `postgresql://`;
- include a host, a user name, and exactly one database name after the host;
- carry no query option other than `sslmode`, which must be one of `disable`, `allow`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca` or `verify-full`.

```sh
CLIENT_DATABASE_URL=postgres://app_user:change-me@db.example.com:5432/app?sslmode=require
```

It must point at a different database from `DATABASE_URL`. A URL that points at the platform database is refused when the connection is checked.

!!! warning
    Setting `CLIENT_DATABASE_URL` replaces a connection saved on the Connections screen the first time the connection is checked, and the saved URL cannot be recovered. If you unset the variable later, enter the URL in the console again.

## Encryption

| Variable | Default | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ENCRYPTION_KEY` | unset | Needed to connect Salesforce | Encrypts the secrets AlgoBridge stores: Salesforce tokens and app credentials, a client database URL saved in the console, and two-step verification keys. Exactly 32 random bytes in base64: generate it with `openssl rand -base64 32`. The app starts without it, but saving a connection or turning on two-step verification is refused. |
| `ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS` | unset | No | Only while rotating keys: the old key. It still decrypts, and never encrypts. Requires `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, and must differ from it. |

### Rotating the encryption key

Rotation has no downtime.

1. Generate a new key with `openssl rand -base64 32`.
2. On every container, move the current key to `ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS`, put the new key in `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, and restart.
3. Re-encrypt every stored secret with the new key:

    ```sh
    docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm app rotate-encryption-key
    ```

    It prints `Re-encrypted N stored secret(s) with key <id>. You can now remove ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS.` It runs in one transaction: if any value cannot be decrypted, nothing changes, and the command names the problem.

4. Remove `ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS` and restart.

## Salesforce

| Variable | Default | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SALESFORCE_CLIENT_ID` | unset | No | The consumer key of the External Client App AlgoBridge signs in through. |
| `SALESFORCE_CLIENT_SECRET` | unset | No | The app's consumer secret. |

Set both or neither. When both are set, they win over credentials saved on the Connections screen, and the screen shows the app as **Set by the deployment**. When neither is set, an admin saves them on the Connections screen instead. The org itself is always connected from the console. See [Salesforce connection](../guides/salesforce-connection.md).

## Registration key

| Variable | Default | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LICENSE_KEY` | unset | No | The instance's registration key, exactly as issued. Surrounding spaces are trimmed. When set, it wins over a key saved on the License panel in Settings, and the panel refuses to save or remove a key. |

A value that is not shaped like a key, including the `<paste-key-here>` placeholder in `deploy/.env.example`, stops the instance at start. A key of the right shape that does not verify does not stop it: the license reads **No key** and sync stays paused. See [Registration keys](/pricing/#registration-keys).

## Sign-in and single sign-on

By default, people sign in with an email and password, plus optional two-step verification. Single sign-on providers are added with `AUTH_PROVIDERS`; several can be active at once. See [Single sign-on](../guides/sso.md) for the provider setup.

### General

| Variable | Default | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `AUTH_PROVIDERS` | `local` | No | Comma-separated sign-in methods: any of `local`, `google`, `microsoft` and `oidc`. Must include `local` unless `AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN=off`. Each SSO provider listed needs its own settings below. |
| `AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN` | `all` | No | Who may sign in with an AlgoBridge password: `all`, `admins` or `off`. `admins` is recommended once SSO works, keeping a break-glass path. `off` removes the password form and needs at least one SSO provider. `create-admin` and admin-issued set-password links work in every mode. |
| `AUTH_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` | empty | No | Comma-separated email domains, such as `example.com`, whose verified SSO users may sign up on first sign-in without an invite. New accounts start as `viewer`. When empty, every new user needs an invite. |

### Google Workspace

Required together when `AUTH_PROVIDERS` includes `google`.

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` | The OAuth client ID. |
| `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` | The OAuth client secret. |
| `GOOGLE_HOSTED_DOMAIN` | Your Workspace domain, such as `example.com`. Only accounts whose hosted domain matches it can sign in, so personal Gmail accounts are always refused. |

### Microsoft Entra ID

Required together when `AUTH_PROVIDERS` includes `microsoft`.

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID` | The application (client) ID. |
| `MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET` | The client secret. |
| `MICROSOFT_TENANT_ID` | Your directory (tenant) ID, as a GUID. `common`, `organizations` and `consumers` are refused, because they would admit accounts from any tenant. |

### Generic OIDC

For Okta, Keycloak, Auth0 and other standard OpenID Connect providers. The first four are required together when `AUTH_PROVIDERS` includes `oidc`.

| Variable | Required with `oidc` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `OIDC_ISSUER` | Yes | The issuer URL. Must be `https://`. AlgoBridge reads the provider's endpoints from its discovery document. |
| `OIDC_CLIENT_ID` | Yes | The client ID. |
| `OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | Yes | The client secret. |
| `OIDC_DISPLAY_NAME` | Yes | The provider name on the sign-in button, shown as "Continue with" followed by this name. |
| `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS` | No, recommended | Comma-separated email domains the provider is trusted for. Checked on every sign-in that matches by email. When empty, any verified email the provider asserts is accepted, and only the invite list keeps out unwanted accounts. |

Domain lists match exactly: a subdomain of an allowed domain is not covered.

## Email

Email is optional. Without it, invite and password-reset links are shown to the admin once, to copy and send, and alerts appear only in the console.

| Variable | Default | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SMTP_URL` | unset | No | The SMTP relay, as an `smtp://` or `smtps://` URL, for example `smtps://user:change-me@mail.example.com:465`. Any provider's SMTP endpoint works. |
| `SMTP_FROM` | unset | With `SMTP_URL` | The sender, for example `AlgoBridge <noreply@example.com>`. |

Set both or neither.

Alert mail uses the same `SMTP_URL` and `SMTP_FROM`. It goes to every active user whose role carries `alerts.receive` (admins, by default), plus any extra addresses entered on the **Alerts** screen, which also sends a test email. The resolved mail waits until the problem has stayed clear for 15 minutes, so a problem that clears and comes straight back does not send a burst of mail.

## Jobs and workers

No environment variable tunes the job engine. Jobs live in the `algobridge_jobs` schema of the platform database named by `DATABASE_URL`, and the only job-related setting you choose per container is `APP_ROLE`. Sync behaviour such as poll intervals is set per mapping in the console. See [Workers and jobs](../guides/workers-and-jobs.md).

## Demo mode

This version reads no demo setting. A demo instance is planned as the same image with a demo flag, but the feature is not built yet.

## Example

A single-container install behind a TLS proxy, with Google sign-in and email. These are the lines in `deploy/.env`; Compose builds `DATABASE_URL` from `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`:

```sh
ALGOBRIDGE_VERSION=0.9.0-rc.1
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<the generated password>
APP_ROLE=all
MIGRATE_ON_BOOT=true
PUBLIC_URL=https://sync.example.com
ENCRYPTION_KEY=<the generated value>
SMTP_URL=smtps://user:change-me@mail.example.com:465
SMTP_FROM=AlgoBridge <noreply@example.com>
AUTH_PROVIDERS=local,google
AUTH_LOCAL_LOGIN=admins
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=change-me
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=change-me
GOOGLE_HOSTED_DOMAIN=example.com
```

---

<!-- https://bridge.cloudalgo.com/docs/getting-started/first-sync/ -->
# Run your first sync

In this page you connect your PostgreSQL database and your Salesforce org, map one Salesforce object to a table, and watch its records load. It follows the console's own screens in the order they ask for things.

You need a running instance with `ENCRYPTION_KEY` set and an admin who can sign in. If you don't have that yet, [install AlgoBridge](install.md) first.

Until both ends are connected, the **Overview** page reads **Connect both ends of the pair**, and the top bar shows each end as not connected. Both steps below happen on **Connections**, under **Instance** in the sidebar. Only admins see it.

<div class="ab-diagram" markdown>
<iframe src="../../assets/diagrams/first-sync.html?embed=1" title="First sync steps" loading="lazy"></iframe>
[Open the first sync steps full size](../assets/diagrams/first-sync.html){ target=_blank }
</div>

## 1. Connect the client database

The client database is your application's PostgreSQL database: the one AlgoBridge creates tables in and syncs. It must not be AlgoBridge's own platform database.

1. Open **Connections**. The **PostgreSQL** panel reads **Not connected**.
2. Paste one connection URL into **Connection URL**, for example:

    ```text
    postgres://app_user:change-me@db.example.com:5432/app?sslmode=require
    ```

3. Click **Test and connect**.

AlgoBridge connects with a 5-second timeout and runs `SELECT version()` before saving anything. If the test fails, nothing is saved, and the error never shows the password. Once connected, the panel lists the host, port, database, user, SSL mode and server version. The URL itself is stored encrypted and never shown again.

The URL accepts one option, `sslmode` (`disable`, `allow`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca` or `verify-full`). Without it the driver's default applies, which does not use SSL. Use `require` or `verify-full` for any database reached over a network.

!!! tip "Set it from the deployment instead"
    You can set `CLIENT_DATABASE_URL` on every container instead of using this screen. It then wins over the screen, which shows the connection as **Set by the deployment (CLIENT_DATABASE_URL)**. See [Client database](../guides/client-database.md) for the trade-offs.

### What the database role needs

AlgoBridge runs every statement in your database itself; there is no "copy this SQL to your DBA" path. Before it creates anything, it checks that the role in the URL can:

- create the `hstore` extension, or find it already installed;
- own the target schema (`algobridge` by default), or create it.

On the first provisioning, the target schema must also be empty. When a check fails, the mapping's Apply panel names the missing grant instead of showing a raw PostgreSQL error.

## 2. Connect Salesforce

AlgoBridge signs in to your org through an External Client App that you create in Salesforce, using OAuth with PKCE. It then acts as the Salesforce user who authorizes it. Use a dedicated integration user, so AlgoBridge's API calls and permissions stay separate from people's.

### Create the External Client App

1. On **Connections**, find the **Salesforce** panel and click **Copy** next to the callback URL. It is your `PUBLIC_URL` followed by `/connections/salesforce/callback`, for example:

    ```text
    https://sync.example.com/connections/salesforce/callback
    ```

2. In Salesforce Setup, open **External Client App Manager** and create a new app. Give it a name and a contact email.
3. Turn on **Enable OAuth** and paste the callback URL as the **Callback URL**.
4. Add the OAuth scopes **Manage user data via APIs (api)** and **Perform requests at any time (refresh_token, offline_access)**.
5. Turn on **Require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)**, and leave **Require secret for Web Server Flow** on.
6. In the app's policies, set **Refresh Token Policy** to keep the token valid until revoked, or allow refresh token rotation.
7. Save, then open **Consumer Key and Secret** and copy both. A new app can take a few minutes to become usable.

### Give AlgoBridge the credentials and connect

1. Back on **Connections**, paste the **Consumer key** and **Consumer secret** and click **Save app credentials**. The secret is stored encrypted and never shown again.
2. Enter the org's **My Domain URL**, such as `https://yourcompany.my.salesforce.com`. A sandbox looks like `https://yourcompany--sandbox.sandbox.my.salesforce.com`. Only hosts ending in `.my.salesforce.com` are accepted.
3. Click **Connect to Salesforce**. Salesforce opens.
4. Sign in as the integration user and allow access.

Salesforce sends you back to **Connections**, which now shows the org, the user AlgoBridge is authorized as, and the org's **API usage today**.

??? note "If Salesforce shows an error"
    | What you see | What to do |
    |---|---|
    | `redirect_uri_mismatch` | The app's Callback URL does not match the instance's. Copy it again from Connections, including `https` and with no trailing slash, and check `PUBLIC_URL`. |
    | The consumer key or secret was rejected | Replace the credentials on Connections. |
    | The app must allow the `refresh_token` scope | Add the scope to the app, wait a few minutes, and connect again. |
    | The connect link expired | More than 10 minutes passed, or the link was already used. Click **Connect to Salesforce** again. |

    More cases are in [Salesforce connection](../guides/salesforce-connection.md).

You can also supply the app's credentials as `SALESFORCE_CLIENT_ID` and `SALESFORCE_CLIENT_SECRET`. When both are set they win over the screen.

### Add the registration key

Every instance needs a free registration key before it syncs. The key must fit the org you just connected: a production key for a production org, the shared sandbox key for a sandbox, the shared Developer Edition key for a Developer Edition org. The License panel names the kind your org needs and links to where to get it.

1. Open **Settings**, and find the **License** panel.
2. Paste the whole key into **Registration key** and click **Save key**. A key that does not verify, or is of the wrong kind for your org, is refused and nothing is saved.
3. The panel reads **Active**. The first 14 days need no status token; after that, paste a current status token from CloudAlgo in the same panel.

Until a fitting key is saved, the Overview shows **Add a registration key** as a setup step, and sync stays paused. Connecting, **Check connection** and the other setup screens work without a key. You can also set the key as `LICENSE_KEY` on every container; it then wins over the panel. See [Registration keys](/pricing/#registration-keys).

## 3. Pick a change source

The change source decides how AlgoBridge learns that Salesforce records changed. Fetching the changed records costs the same whichever you pick; the source decides what it costs to find out. Choose it on **Connections**, in the **Change detection** panel.

| Source | Installs in your org | Cost to learn about changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Composite polling** (default) | Nothing. | One API request per five objects per poll. |
| **Apex probe** | The AlgoBridge Apex bundle: one read-only class, its tests and a permission set. | One API request per poll for up to 90 objects. |
| **Change notifier** | The same bundle, a one-time pairing, and two Flows per synced object. Needs AlgoBridge reachable from Salesforce over HTTPS. | Zero, plus one fallback poll an hour. |

For a first sync, keep **Composite polling**. It needs nothing installed, and you can switch later without touching your mappings.

To use the Apex probe instead:

1. In **Change detection**, click **Deploy bundle**. The deploy runs in the background and the panel shows *Deploy succeeded* or *Deploy failed*. The integration user needs **Modify All Data** (or **Modify Metadata Through Metadata API Functions**) and **Author Apex** to deploy.
2. In Salesforce Setup, assign the **AlgoBridge Integration** permission set (`algobridge_Integration`) to the integration user, and to no one else.
3. Click **Use this source** on the **Apex probe** card. AlgoBridge makes one status call to the bundle and saves your choice only if the bundle answers.

The change notifier takes a few more steps. See [Change sources](../guides/change-sources.md) and [Apex bundle](../guides/apex-bundle.md).

## 4. Add a mapping

A mapping says which Salesforce object syncs into which PostgreSQL table, with which fields. Members and admins can create mappings.

### Check the instance settings first

Open **Mappings**, under **Sync** in the sidebar. The **Settings** panel holds two instance-wide choices:

- **Target schema**: the PostgreSQL schema AlgoBridge creates its tables in. The default is `algobridge`. You can change it only until the first mapping exists.
- **Write algorithm**: how changes are sent to Salesforce. **Ordered Writes (recommended)** is the default. **Merged Writes** merges several changes to one record before sending, and reorders parents ahead of children. You can change it at any time.

### Choose the object

1. Click **New mapping**. The first step, **Choose object**, lists the objects in your org.
2. Search for the object, for example `Account`, and click **Choose**. Click **Refresh** if a new object is missing from the list.

### Choose fields and settings

The second step, **Choose fields and settings**, opens the editor. The table name comes from the object's API name, lowercased, and is fixed once the mapping exists.

| Panel | What to choose |
|---|---|
| **Direction** | **Read-only**: Salesforce changes sync to PostgreSQL, and PostgreSQL never writes back. **Read-write**: changes sync both ways. Read-write is unavailable for objects Salesforce reports as neither createable nor updateable. |
| **When both sides change** | Read-write only. **Salesforce wins** (the default), **PostgreSQL wins**, or **Latest change wins**. See [Conflicts](../concepts/conflicts.md). |
| **Matching key** | An optional External ID field, chosen from fields that are External ID and Unique in Salesforce. Without one, rows inserted in PostgreSQL risk creating duplicates. |
| **Polling** | **Fastest** and **Slowest** poll intervals in minutes: 5 and 30 by default, each between 2 and 60. The interval stretches toward the slowest while nothing changes, and snaps back to the fastest when something does. |
